slides.title: Think before you click
bullets: Phishing emails pretend to come from someone you trust to steal passwords, money or data.
Watch for urgency, threats, prizes or anything you were not expecting.
When in doubt, don't click. Call the sender at a number you already know.
more: Phishing is the most common way attackers get into a business. The message looks like it comes from Microsoft, a bank, a shipping company, a vendor or even a coworker.
Red flags: a sense of urgency ("your account will be closed today"), a request for a password or payment, a link that does not match the company, bad grammar, or an attachment you did not expect.
If something feels off, stop. Do not click links or open attachments. Contact the person or company using a phone number or website you already trust, or call NMS.

slides.title: Spoofing: the name is not the sender
bullets: Anyone can type any display name, like "Microsoft Support" or your boss's name.
Always check the real email address, not just the name.
Look-alike addresses swap letters: micros0ft.com, rnicrosoft.com, paypa1.com.
more: Spoofing is when a scammer makes a message look like it comes from someone else. The most common trick is the display name: the email shows "Microsoft 365 Support" or your manager's name, but the real address behind it is a stranger's Gmail or a fake domain.

Look-alike domains change one character so it looks right at a glance: a zero instead of an O (micros0ft.com), "rn" instead of "m" (rnicrosoft.com), a 1 instead of an L (paypa1.com), or extra words (microsoft-alerts.co).
On a phone, tap the sender's name to see the full address. On a computer, hover over the name. Also check the Reply-To: if you reply and the address changes, it is a scam.
Phone numbers and text messages can be spoofed too. A call that shows your bank's name is not proof it is your bank.

slides.title: New bank details? Call to verify
bullets: Scammers spoof or hijack vendor emails and send "new" bank or wire instructions.
Never change payment information based only on an email or a PDF.
Call the vendor at the number on file, not the one in the email.
more: This scam is called Business Email Compromise (BEC). A criminal gets into a vendor's or client's mailbox, or makes a look-alike address, and waits for a real invoice. Then they send a message saying the bank account has changed.
The email looks normal, uses the right names and may continue a real conversation. The only change is where the money goes. Once a wire or ACH is sent, it is very hard to get back.
Rule: any change to bank details, any urgent wire, or any payment to a new account is confirmed by phone, using a number you already had on file, before money moves.

slides.title: Gift card requests are a scam
bullets: "I'm in a meeting, buy gift cards and send me the codes" is a classic scam.
Real managers, companies and government agencies never ask for payment in gift cards.
Verify in person or by phone before you buy anything.
more: The message usually looks like it comes from the owner or a manager, by email or text: "Are you busy? I need a favor." Then it asks you to buy gift cards for a client or an event and send pictures of the codes.
Once the codes are sent, the money is gone. Gift cards can't be traced or refunded.
If you get a request like this, do not reply to the message. Call the person at the number you know or ask them in person.

slides.title: Never share your code
bullets: Verification codes are the last lock on your account. Never read them to anyone.
No real bank, Microsoft or IT support will ask you for a code.
Got a sign-in request you didn't start? Deny it and tell NMS.
more: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) sends a code or an approval request to your phone. If a scammer already has your password, that code is the only thing stopping them.
Scammers call pretending to be your bank or IT support and say they will "send you a code to verify you". If you read it to them, they are in your account.
If your phone asks you to approve a sign-in that you did not start, someone has your password. Tap Deny, then call NMS so we can change it.

slides.title: Check the link before you sign in
bullets: Fake login pages look exactly like Microsoft 365, banks or shipping sites.
Hover over links and read the real address before you click.
Sign in only on sites you opened yourself, never from an email link.
more: A phishing link takes you to a copy of a real login page. Everything looks the same, but the password you type goes to the attacker.

Before you click, hover over the link (or press and hold on a phone) and read the address. The real company name must be right before the first single slash, for example login.microsoftonline.com, not microsoft.login-secure.co.
The lock icon (HTTPS) only means the connection is encrypted. Fake sites have it too. The address is what matters.
Safest habit: open the site yourself from a bookmark or by typing the address.

slides.title: Unexpected attachment? Don't open it
bullets: Fake invoices, shipping notices and voicemails often hide malware.
Be extra careful with .zip, .html and .iso files and "Enable content" buttons.
Not expecting it? Confirm with the sender first.
more: Attackers attach files that look like invoices, purchase orders, scanned documents, voicemails or shipping labels. Opening them can install malware or ransomware.
Higher risk files: .zip, .iso, .html or .htm, .js, .exe, and Office documents that ask you to click "Enable Content" or "Enable Editing".
If you were not expecting a file, check with the sender by phone or a new message before opening it.

slides.title: Fake "verify" and "fix it" pages
bullets: Some pages ask you to press Windows + R and paste a command to "verify" or "fix" something.
That is a trap that installs malware. Close the page.
Real websites never ask you to run commands on your computer.
more: A growing scam shows a fake CAPTCHA ("Verify you are human") or a fake error message with steps: press Windows + R, press Ctrl + V, press Enter. The page has already copied a malicious command to your clipboard.
Following the steps runs the attacker's program with your permissions. No real website, CAPTCHA or browser update works this way.
If you see this, close the browser tab. If you already ran it, disconnect from the network and call NMS right away.

slides.title: Texts and calls can be scams too
bullets: Fake texts about packages, tolls or bank alerts push you to a link.
Caller ID can be faked. Hang up and call the official number.
Never give passwords, codes or card numbers over the phone.
more: Smishing (SMS phishing) and vishing (voice phishing) use the same tricks as email: urgency and a link or a number to call.
Common examples: a package on hold, an unpaid toll, a locked bank card, a refund, or "Microsoft support" saying your computer is infected.
Do not use the link or number in the message. Hang up and call the company using the number on its official website or on the back of your card.

slides.title: Something looks wrong? Report it
bullets: Use the Report button in Outlook, or call NMS. Don't forward it to coworkers.
Clicked something by mistake? Tell us right away. Minutes matter.
You will never get in trouble for reporting.
more: Reporting a suspicious message helps protect everyone in the company. In Outlook, use Report > Phishing (or Report Message). If you are not sure, call NMS.
If you clicked a link, typed your password or opened an attachment, call us immediately. The sooner we know, the faster we can lock the account and stop the damage.
Nobody gets in trouble for reporting, even if it turns out to be safe.

slides.title: Use strong, unique passwords
bullets: Use a passphrase: four or more random words, 16 characters or longer.
Never reuse your work password anywhere else.
Use a password manager and turn on multi-factor authentication.
more: Long passphrases are easier to remember and harder to crack than short complex passwords. Example of the idea: four unrelated words with a number or symbol.
When a website is hacked, criminals try the same email and password on other sites. A unique password for each account stops that.
A password manager remembers them for you. Multi-factor authentication adds a second lock in case a password leaks.
